abstract: |
  Can the physical shape of a writing support encode, and when applied at
  sufficient scale reveal, the institutional history of the civilizations that
  produced it? We address this question through a systematic,
  computational-diplomatic analysis of 94,936 cuneiform tablet images from the
  Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI) spanning 21 historical periods
  across approximately 3,300 years (3500 to 64 BCE). Rather than examining
  textual content or inscription style, we focus exclusively on the
  two-dimensional silhouette of each tablet, treating shape as a primary
  historical signal independent of surface detail. Four main findings emerge.
  First, we document a statistically robust diachronic shift from predominantly
  portrait to landscape tablet orientation across three millennia — the first
  large-scale quantitative evidence for this diplomatic evolution — and show via
  geographic decomposition that the shift is real and widespread across production
  sites rather than a sampling artifact. Second, binary silhouettes alone carry
  approximately 86% of the period-classification information present in full
  grayscale images: a fine-tuned ResNet50 achieves 71% macro-F1 across 21 classes
  on grayscale images and 61% on masked silhouettes, against a 4.8% random
  baseline, with highest performance for periods of intense institutional
  standardization (Ur III: 87%; Neo-Assyrian: 95%). Third, a coefficient-of-variation
  analysis reveals a standardization scale running from the tightly uniform Ur III
  state (CV = 0.251) through the institutionally plural Neo-Babylonian period
  (CV = 0.807) to the Achaemenid empire, where the central half of the tablet
  population occupies an exceptionally narrow landscape band (IQR = 0.150),
  reflecting an imperial orientation norm imposed on a diverse scribal landscape.
  Fourth, a Variational Autoencoder with a 12-dimensional bottleneck separates the
  diachronic drift in tablet form (bounding-box fill efficiency, increasing over
  time) from the categorical identity of diplomatic traditions (height/width ratio,
  which distinguishes traditions non-monotonically), enabling interpretable
  visualization and diplomatic genealogy analysis across periods and genres.
  Together these results constitute a framework for computational diplomatics
  that scales traditional document-format analysis across corpora orders of
  magnitude larger than expert review permits.

runningauthor: "Gordin, Kapon Epshtain, and Fire"

significance: |
  Clay tablets are more than the texts they carry: their physical shape reflects
  the institutional norms, scribal training practices, and administrative cultures
  of the civilizations that produced them. Yet the systematic study of tablet
  format, known as diplomatics, has remained qualitative and limited to small
  corpora. We apply advanced machine learning to 94,936 cuneiform images spanning
  3,300 years, demonstrating for the first time that tablet shape alone carries
  measurable historical signal sufficient to identify a document's period of
  origin. We uncover a three-millennium shift from portrait to landscape orientation,
  confirmed across geographically distributed production sites from Nippur to Kalhu.
  A standardization scale derived from coefficient-of-variation analysis reveals
  that the Ur III state (2,110–2,003 BCE) produced the most morphologically uniform
  tablets in 3,300 years of cuneiform production, while the Achaemenid empire
  (539–330 BCE) imposed a distinct landscape norm with exceptional consistency in
  its central tendency. A Variational Autoencoder separates the diachronic drift
  in tablet form from the categorical identity of diplomatic traditions, making
  implicit scribal norms computationally explicit and recoverable at scale.
  This methodology is transferable to any ancient document corpus where material
  form encodes cultural history.

\dropcap{T}he clay tablet, the dominant writing support of the ancient Near East
for over three thousand years, is more than a vehicle for text. Its shape,
proportions, and material form are themselves historical documents. The systematic
study of document format, known as *diplomatics*, was established as a formal
scholarly discipline by Jean Mabillon's *De Re Diplomatica* (1681)
[@mabillonDeReDiplomatica1681], which set out criteria for
authenticating medieval charters through their external features: script type,
formulaic structure, material support, and seal impressions. The discipline was
institutionalized in the nineteenth century, through the work of Theodor von
Sickel and others on Latin administrative records, as proof that the physical form
of a document encodes the institutional context of its production, often more
reliably than its text. Scholars of cuneiform have consistently recognized this
principle: dominant text genres carry consistent shapes; periods of centralized
administration produce more homogeneous document formats than periods of
political fragmentation [@charpinReadingWriting2010; @charpinWritingLaw2010;
@hacklMaterialienZurUrkundenlehre2013; @jursaDiplomaticsLateBabylonian2021;
@cancik-kirschbaumMiddleAssyrian2012; @radnerRelationFormat1995]. Yet despite
nearly two centuries of cuneiform scholarship [@walkerCuneiform1987;
@woodsIntroductionVisibleLanguage2010], the diplomatic study of tablet shape has
remained necessarily qualitative and bounded by the limits of expert inspection
across small corpora. The mass digitization of cuneiform collections now makes a
different approach possible.

**Diplomatics and the problem of tablet dating.** Cuneiform, the logo-syllabic
writing system impressed with a reed stylus on clay, finds its origins in ancient
Mesopotamia during the late fourth millennium BCE
[@woodsIntroductionVisibleLanguage2010]. The Sumerians, followed by the Elamites,
Akkadians, Hurrians, Hittites, and many other ancient Near Eastern cultures used
this medium to produce vast archives of administrative, legal, literary, and
scientific texts, many surviving on durable clay that has withstood the harsh
Middle Eastern climate [@walkerCuneiform1987]. Dating individual tablets to their
historical period of origin is among the most consequential tasks in cuneiform
studies, yet it relies on a confluence of criteria that is difficult to standardize:
clay composition, size, shape, sign forms, ductus, genre conventions, associated
finds, and stratigraphic context. Significant discrepancies among scholars occur
even for tablets from periods with abundant comparanda, and assumptions embedded
in existing date assignments may themselves introduce circularity when those
assignments are used as training labels for automated methods
[@chenDistributionShift2024]. Archaeomagnetic measurement of
baked clay offers a promising independent chronological approach, demonstrated on
inscribed bricks from Mesopotamia spanning the third through first millennia BCE
[@howlandArchaeomagneticBricks2023], though its application
remains constrained to thermally altered material and regional reference curves.

The physical shape of a tablet, what diplomatic scholarship calls its *format*,
is one of the most telling and underexploited dating criteria. Scholars have long
noted that format correlates with genre, archive, period, and institutional
context. Radner demonstrated that Neo-Assyrian letter tablets maintain among the
most consistent formats in the cuneiform corpus, regardless of archive provenance
[@radnerRelationFormat1995]; Hackl documented systematic shape shifts in the Late
Babylonian Tattannu archive as functions of administrative function and diachronic
change [@hacklMaterialienZurUrkundenlehre2013]; Jursa and colleagues have analyzed
the diplomatic norms of Late Babylonian archival texts as evidence for
institutional practice and its transformation across the first millennium BCE
[@jursaDiplomaticsLateBabylonian2021]. What has been lacking is a method to extend
these observations systematically, across the full chronological span of cuneiform
writing, across all regions and genres represented in modern collections, and using
criteria explicit and reproducible enough to constitute scientific evidence.

Crucially, tablet shape was not accidental. The physical preparation of clay
before inscription, its wedging, forming, and shaping, was itself a component of
scribal education in ancient Mesopotamia. Old Babylonian scribal curricula,
attested most clearly at Nippur and other centers, included graduated exercises
in which tablet format varied systematically by pedagogical stage and genre
[@veldhuisLevelsLiteracy2011; @veldhuisCuneiformTabletEducational1996;
@delneroArchivesLibrariesOld2019]. Tablets produced by a bureaucratic institution
such as the Ur III state (2,110 to 2,003 BCE) show remarkable morphological
consistency, reflecting not only centralized administrative norms but the
standardized training of the scribal workforce that implemented them
[@steinkellerHistoryTexts2017; @englund_administrative_1988]. Shape consistency
is therefore a proxy for institutional control; shape diversity marks competing
scribal traditions or political fragmentation.

**Distant viewing applied to cuneiform.** Recent advances in digitization have
transformed the scale of available cuneiform data. The Cuneiform Digital Library
Initiative (CDLI) now catalogues over 360,000 records from museums and collections
worldwide, with over 94,000 photographically documented tablets accompanied by
expert-assigned period and genre metadata [@cdliContributors2024].
Chen et al. [@chenCuneiML2023] assembled the first large-scale
ML-ready dataset from this corpus (38,947 tablets with paired images,
transliterations, and metadata), establishing baseline period-classification
performance of up to 97.66% accuracy using combined image and text features.
Subsequent analysis by the same group revealed, however, that such figures
substantially overstate real-world generalizability: when tested on held-out
museum collections rather than a random split, ResNet-based classifiers decline
from approximately 80% to 35% macro-F1, driven by photographic confounds that
co-vary with institutional provenance [@chenDistributionShift2024].
These findings underscore both the promise and the methodological hazards of
large-scale computational approaches to cuneiform dating.

The appropriate framework for such analysis is what Arnold and Tilton term
*distant viewing*: the systematic, explicit, and reproducible application of
computational tools to large visual corpora, designed to reveal patterns invisible
at the scale of close reading while remaining anchored in domain expertise
[@arnoldTiltonDistantViewing2019]. Unlike distant reading of
text, which operates directly on an existing symbolic code, distant viewing
requires the researcher to construct a code system first, to decide which visual
features to measure, which to discard, and how to operationalize implicit expert
knowledge into explicit computational criteria. In our application, this code
system is deliberately minimal: we represent each tablet as a binary silhouette,
a black-and-white outline stripped of all surface detail, sign forms, and
photographic texture. This reduction is both a methodological choice and an
empirical test. If shape alone, independent of inscription content, carries
sufficient historical signal to distinguish periods, then shape is doing
diplomatic work. As we demonstrate, it does, and the degree to which it does is
itself historically informative. Critically, binary masks discard the scanning
hardware signatures, lighting conditions, and color profiles that drive
collection-specific overfitting in prior studies, making the silhouette approach
architecturally more robust to the distribution shift documented by Chen et al.
[@chenDistributionShift2024].

**Research questions and scope.** This study addresses three interlocking
questions. How much period-specific information is preserved in tablet shape
alone, independent of textual or stylistic content? Which shape features are most
historically discriminating, and can these be rendered interpretable in terms that
connect to established diplomatic scholarship? What does the aggregate distribution
of tablet shapes across 3,300 years reveal about the long-term evolution of
cuneiform document culture?

To address these questions we assemble the largest dataset yet used for this
purpose: 94,936 tablet images from the CDLI catalogue [@cdliContributors2024],
representing 21 distinct historical periods and the
principal text genres of cuneiform scholarship (@fig-samples). Our analytical
pipeline proceeds in three stages. We first perform exploratory analysis of
height-to-width ratios as a minimal shape descriptor, establishing period-level
distributions and testing whether a single geometric ratio carries classifiable
information. We then train and evaluate a series of period-classification models
of increasing sophistication, from a decision tree on ratios to a fine-tuned
ResNet50 on full silhouettes, comparing performance across grayscale and masked
image representations to quantify shape's independent contribution. Finally, we
employ a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) [@kingmaVAE2013] to
decompress each tablet's shape into a 12-dimensional interpretable feature space,
enabling hierarchical clustering, diachronic trajectory analysis, and interactive
visualization through two purpose-built digital tools. VAE-based latent space
analysis has established precedents in archaeological shape analysis, including
the unsupervised typological study of ceramic assemblages
[@parisottoUnsupervised2022;
@cardarelliDeep2022] and the broader tradition of geometric
morphometrics applied to artifacts [@sliceGeometricMorphometrics2007;
@schlagerChapter9Morpho2017]; we apply this approach not for image generation but
as a structured analytical lens for interpreting tablet morphology across periods
and genres. @tbl-related-work situates the present study in relation to the two
most relevant prior computational studies, both using CDLI data.

## Dataset and Preprocessing

**CDLI corpus: scope and representativeness.** The Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative
(CDLI) is the primary open-access repository of cuneiform artifact records,
maintaining catalogues for over 360,000 objects from museums and private collections
worldwide [@cdliContributors2024]. Of these, approximately
100,000 entries are accompanied by photographic documentation of sufficient quality
for automated analysis. After filtering to entries with usable images, confirmed
period assignments drawn from the CDLI metadata taxonomy, and at least 50 specimens
per period class (to permit meaningful classifier training and evaluation), our
working corpus comprised **94,936 tablet images** spanning **21 distinct historical
periods** from approximately 3500 to 64 BCE (@fig-samples). These images represent
the principal text-producing cultures of the ancient Near East, including Sumerian,
Akkadian, Old Babylonian, Middle Babylonian, Middle Assyrian, Neo-Assyrian,
Neo-Babylonian, Achaemenid, and Hellenistic scribal traditions, among others
(@tbl-periods).

The corpus is not a representative sample of cuneiform production in antiquity.
It reflects the accumulated priorities of two centuries of excavation, the
acquisition histories of major collecting institutions, and the digitization
capacities of CDLI's partner museums. Four period categories, Ur III (2110 to 2003
BCE), Neo-Assyrian (911 to 612 BCE), Old Babylonian (2000 to 1600 BCE), and Middle
Babylonian (1400 to 1000 BCE), account for approximately 63% of the total corpus.
These periods are heavily represented not because ancient productivity was
concentrated in them but because the sites that produced their tablets (Nippur,
Girsu, Nineveh, Nimrud) were excavated intensively in the nineteenth and early
twentieth centuries and their contents distributed to institutions that have
subsequently digitized at scale. Periods such as the Early Dynastic (2900 to 2350
BCE) and the Neo-Elamite (770 to 539 BCE) are represented by far fewer specimens,
and our models' performance in these categories necessarily reflects this data
scarcity. We return to this limitation in the Discussion.

**Why ratios? The absence of absolute dimensions.** The most immediately useful
physical descriptor of a tablet's format is its actual height and width in
centimetres. This information would allow direct comparison across photographic
conditions, camera distances, and image resolutions. However, **the CDLI catalogue
does not systematically record physical dimensions for the majority of its entries**,
and such measurements, when present, have been entered with varying conventions
and levels of completeness across contributing institutions. We therefore work
exclusively with height-to-width pixel ratios derived from the photographic images,
which encode relative proportions rather than absolute measurements. This is a
genuine limitation: a tablet photographed at close range occupies the same pixel
area as a much larger tablet photographed from a greater distance, and their ratios
will be identical even though their physical formats differ.

The consequence is that distributional overlap between period categories in ratio
space is substantial. Administrative tablets from the Ur III and Old Babylonian
periods overlap considerably in their ratio distributions (@fig-ratio-dist), as
do many other neighbouring periods. That our classifiers nonetheless achieve
performance far above the 4.8% chance baseline under these conditions is therefore
a stronger indicator of genuine morphological differentiation than the absolute
accuracy figures alone would suggest: the models are detecting real signal in a
measurement regime that systematically discards much of the available information.
The availability of standardized physical dimension data, ideally collected through
photogrammetric imaging protocols, would substantially reduce this ambiguity and
is a priority for future data collection by the cuneiform studies community.

**Silhouette extraction and preprocessing pipeline.** CDLI images vary
substantially in their photographic conditions: background colour (white, grey,
black), scale bar presence, illumination angle, and image resolution. To remove
these photographic confounds and isolate morphological information, we applied a
uniform silhouette extraction pipeline to all 94,936 images. Each image was first
converted to grayscale and subjected to Otsu's thresholding
[@otsuThresholdSelectionMethod1979] to produce a binary
foreground-background mask. Morphological closing was applied to fill small holes
from surface engraving and damage. The binary mask was then processed to extract
the **largest connected component**, which in the overwhelming majority of cases
corresponds to the main tablet body. The resulting binary silhouette retains the
tablet's two-dimensional outline and overall proportions while discarding cuneiform
signs, surface texture, clay colour, photographic background, and any scale bar
artefacts.

This silhouette extraction step serves two purposes beyond standardization. It
directly operationalizes the diplomatic concept of tablet format — the shape as a
historical object independent of the text inscribed on it — and it removes the
scanning-hardware signatures and institution-specific photographic conventions
that, as Chen et al. have demonstrated, drive collection-specific overfitting in
models trained on full grayscale images [@chenDistributionShift2024].
Binary silhouettes are architecturally more robust to the kind of distribution
shift that degrades cross-collection generalization, because they discard precisely
the features (lighting, colour profile, scanner calibration) that differ most
between institutional collections while preserving the features (shape,
proportions, outline) that reflect the object's own historical properties.

**Which tablet views are included, and what the largest-component extraction
does.** CDLI photographs vary in what they show. Some images present only a single
face of the tablet (the obverse or reverse); others show multiple faces on a single
canvas in a composite layout, with the obverse, reverse, and one or more lateral
edges arranged side by side. This variation is not recorded in CDLI metadata and
must be inferred from the image itself. For our **ratio analysis and the
height-to-width measurements** reported in the Results, we use images as delivered
by CDLI, applying the largest connected component to select the dominant visible
region when multiple components are detected. This approach isolates the largest
contiguous area, which is typically the main face of the tablet, but it is
imperfect: for composite images where the obverse and reverse are presented at
equal size and separated by a narrow gap, the algorithm may select one face
arbitrarily, or may retain a merged shape that does not correspond to any single
physical surface.

For the **ResNet50 period-classification models**, we distinguish two experimental
conditions explicitly. In the *grayscale* condition, models receive the full
photographic image, resized and normalized, without mask extraction; this condition
therefore includes whatever multi-face composite layouts are present in the CDLI
source data. In the *masked silhouette* condition, models receive only the binary
mask after largest-component extraction, which partially mitigates the composite
image problem by discarding all but the dominant connected region. The comparison
between these two conditions — 71% macro-F1 for grayscale versus 61% for masked
silhouettes — establishes both the cost of discarding photographic surface
information and, by complement, the proportion of period-distinctive information
carried by shape alone. For the **VAE**, all training used the masked silhouette
representation, so that the latent space encodes shape features rather than
photographic properties.

A known confound in the **administrative genre clustering** (discussed in Results)
is that administrative tablets are disproportionately represented by composite
images showing obverse, reverse, and edge views on a single canvas. For such
images, the silhouette of the composite layout is wider than the silhouette of
any individual tablet face, and this artifactual widening may contribute to the
landscape-leaning appearance of administrative tablets in some periods. We flag
this explicitly where it affects interpretation and note that resolution of this
confound requires either manual annotation of image type or the adoption of
standardized single-face photography as a community norm.

## Results

### The three-millennium shift: from portrait to landscape

The most consistent finding across all measurement strategies is a directional,
millennia-long reorientation of cuneiform tablets from portrait to landscape format.
Across the 94,936-tablet corpus, the median height-to-width ratio falls from 1.125
in the Ur III period (2,110–2,003 BCE) — the most tablet-rich period in the 2nd
millennium — to 0.741 in the Neo-Babylonian period (625–539 BCE) and 0.786 in the
Achaemenid period (539–330 BCE), a shift of approximately −0.27 in log-ratio space
over the 2nd-to-1st-millennium transition (@fig-ratio-period). This trend is not
an artifact of a single measurement approach: the same directional signal emerges
from physical pixel-ratio analysis, from image-derived pixel ratios in a larger
pixel-ratio subsample, and from the most diachronically sensitive dimension of the
VAE latent space (Spearman ρ = +0.655, *p* = 0.001; see below). Three independent
measurement regimes pointing to the same transition constitute strong evidence that
this is a genuine property of the cuneiform corpus and not a photographic or
analytical artifact.

The shift is not abrupt. The clearest inflection occurs between the Old Babylonian
(1,900–1,600 BCE; median h/w = 1.282) and the Middle Babylonian period (1,400–1,000
BCE; median h/w = 1.000), when the population of tablets first achieves rough
geometric neutrality — that is, an equal mix of portrait and landscape orientations
around the isometric h/w = 1.0 boundary. The Middle Elamite period (1,450–1,050 BCE)
is a notable outlier in the 2nd millennium, with a median h/w of 0.863, placing it
squarely in landscape territory two to three centuries before Babylonian and Assyrian
corpora make the equivalent transition. This early landscape norm in the Elamite
administrative tradition — attested primarily at Susa and at the Achaemenid-era
Persepolis Fortification Archive — is historically significant and will be revisited
in the Discussion.

**Standardization across periods.** The portrait-to-landscape transition is not
simply a shift in median format; it is accompanied by varying degrees of
standardization — the concentration of a period's tablets around a modal format
— that encode the degree of institutional control over scribal practice. We operationalize
standardization as the coefficient of variation (CV = σ/μ) of the h/w ratio within
each period [@eerkensStandardizationArtifact2000], which scales dispersion to the
mean and therefore permits comparison across periods with different absolute
ratio levels. The resulting standardization scale runs from Ur III (CV = 0.251),
the most morphologically homogeneous period in the corpus, through the Early
Old Babylonian (CV = 0.274) and Proto-Elamite (CV = 0.279), to the Neo-Babylonian
(CV = 0.807), which shows the greatest dispersion of any period with substantial
representation (@fig-cv-standardization).

The Ur III result is consistent with the abundant documentary evidence for
centralized scribal training and bureaucratic uniformity under the Third Dynasty
of Ur [@steinkellerHistoryTexts2017; @englund_administrative_1988]. The remarkable
morphological consistency of Ur III administrative tablets — many produced in the
same scribal offices at Nippur, Girsu, Puzriš-Dagan, and Umma — reflects not
only institutional format norms but the standardized curriculum of the *edubba'a*,
the scribal school, in which the physical formation of the clay tablet was a
component of professional training [@veldhuisLevelsLiteracy2011;
@delneroArchivesLibrariesOld2019]. When the curriculum was uniform and the
administering institution was a single state, the tablets it produced were uniform.

Achaemenid tablets (539–330 BCE) present a more complex standardization picture.
Their pixel IQR of 0.150 — the second-tightest in the entire corpus after Ur III
(IQR = 0.180 in the same pixel-ratio analysis) — establishes that the central
half of the Achaemenid tablet population occupies an exceptionally narrow landscape
band. This indicates a strong attractor toward landscape orientation, consistent
with a well-enforced imperial format norm. At the same time, the overall CV remains
elevated relative to Ur III, driven by outlier tablets spanning a wide range of
ratios. The appropriate characterization is not global standardization but
*orientation standardization*: Achaemenid scribal culture had internalized landscape
as the correct format for administrative documents while retaining heterogeneous
practice for exceptional document types.

The Neo-Babylonian CV of 0.807 reflects a different institutional reality. Neo-Babylonian
tablets emerge from a diverse assemblage of institutional contexts — Babylonian temple
archives, private merchant and banking archives, royal administrative records — each
with somewhat different format conventions [@jursaDiplomaticsLateBabylonian2021;
@waerzeggers_marduk-remanni_2014]. The high CV is therefore not evidence of
scribal freedom but of institutional fragmentation: there was no single authority
standardizing format across all tablet-producing contexts simultaneously.

**Cognitive templates and "fixed balance."** The bimodal character of the overall
tablet-shape distribution — a portrait cluster centered around h/w ≈ 1.1–1.3 in
the 3rd and early 2nd millennium, and a landscape cluster around h/w ≈ 0.75–0.85
from the late 2nd millennium onward — suggests that cuneiform scribal culture did
not treat tablet proportions as a continuous variable to be freely adjusted with
each commission. Instead, it operated with discrete preferred proportions, analogous
to what scholars of manuscript production have termed *fixed balance*: pre-determined
target aspect ratios that scribes reproduced across thousands of individually
hand-formed tablets, regardless of text length or content
[@georgeGeometryEarlyQuranic2010; @stokesPalaeographyDigitalAge2015]. The portrait
template of the 3rd and early 2nd millennium and the landscape template of the
1st millennium are not endpoints of a continuum: they are distinct attractors
in ratio space, and the transition between them constitutes one of the most
consequential shifts in the material culture of ancient writing.

### Period classification: the historical signal in silhouette shape {#sec-classification}

A series of period-classification experiments tests whether the diachronic shape
variation visible in ratio distributions constitutes sufficient historical signal for
automated period identification — and, critically, how much of that signal is carried
by the binary silhouette alone versus the full photographic image.

We trained and evaluated three classifiers of increasing sophistication. A decision
tree operating on the scalar h/w ratio achieves 30.1% macro-F1 across 21 period
classes, against a 4.8% random baseline, confirming that even the minimal one-number
shape descriptor carries substantial period-predictive information. A convolutional
neural network (CNN) trained on masked binary silhouettes achieves 50% macro-F1.
A fine-tuned ResNet50 [@heResNet2016] achieves **71% macro-F1 on full grayscale images**
and **61% macro-F1 on masked binary silhouettes** across 21 period classes
(@tbl-model-performance).

The ratio of silhouette-to-grayscale performance (61/71 ≈ 0.86) defines what we
term the *shape information retention fraction*: **binary silhouettes alone carry
approximately 86% of the period-classification signal present in full photographic
images**. The remaining 14% is contributed by photographic surface properties —
clay colour, sign density, texture — that are discarded by the binarization step.
This result has two important implications. First, tablet shape is the dominant
carrier of period-specific information even in photographs that retain all surface
detail. Second, the silhouette approach, by discarding precisely those
institution-specific photographic properties that Chen et al. have shown to drive
cross-collection overfitting [@chenDistributionShift2024], achieves
architectural robustness at a cost of only 14% in classification performance.

Per-period performance is strongly modulated by institutional standardization.
Ur III achieves approximately 87% F1 and Neo-Assyrian approximately 95% — the two
periods with the tightest CV in the corpus and the most extensively documented
format conventions [@radnerRelationFormat1995; @steinkellerHistoryTexts2017].
The confusion matrix reveals systematic ambiguity between adjacent periods with
similar format conventions — most notably between Early Old Babylonian and Old
Babylonian, where the transition is gradual and the scholarly periodization boundary
is itself imprecise. The classifier's confusion in this zone reflects a genuine
empirical property of the corpus rather than a modelling failure: where scholars
disagree about periodization, the tablets' physical shapes also fail to separate
cleanly.

| Model | Input | Macro-F1 |
|---|---|---|
| Decision tree | h/w ratio | 30.1% |
| CNN | Masked silhouette | 50.0% |
| ResNet50 | Full grayscale | 71.0% |
| ResNet50 | Masked silhouette | 61.0% |
| Random baseline | — | 4.8% |

: Period classification performance across 21 classes. Shape information retention
  fraction: 61/71 ≈ 86%. {#tbl-model-performance}

### VAE: interpretable shape features and diplomatic genealogies {#sec-vae}

Variational Autoencoder analysis with a 12-dimensional bottleneck reveals the
geometric structure underlying the diachronic and cross-period variation observed
in the ratio analysis, and yields interpretable shape features that map onto
established diplomatic categories.

**Discrimination versus trend: two separable functions.** The 12 VAE dimensions
play distinct historical roles, revealed by two complementary statistics: the
Kruskal-Wallis η² measures each dimension's ability to discriminate between the 21
period categories (analogous to a measure of between-period variance), and the
Spearman ρ against chronological rank measures monotonic diachronic trend. For
most dimensions, these two statistics diverge: a dimension can strongly discriminate
between periods without trending across time, and a dimension can trend consistently
without being a strong period discriminator.

Dimension X7 illustrates the first case: η² = 0.435 (large effect, the strongest
discriminator in the bottleneck) but ρ = −0.430, *p* = 0.052, with no significant
linear trend. Dimension X2 illustrates the second: η² = 0.078 (medium effect,
ranking fifth of twelve in discriminative power) but ρ = +0.655, *p* = 0.001,
the strongest monotonic diachronic signal in the latent space.
A secondary trend dimension, X8, contributes ρ = −0.573, *p* = 0.007 (@fig-vae-eta2-rho).

**Physical meaning: latent traversal.** The physical feature controlled by each
dimension was determined by decoding synthetic tablet images at eleven evenly spaced
points along its ±2σ range, measuring five geometric descriptors (height/width ratio,
area fraction, solidity, compactness, eccentricity) on the decoded silhouettes, and
identifying which descriptor changes most monotonically along the traversal axis. The
results, confirmed across three genre baselines (Administrative, Literary, Legal), are
as follows [@fig-vae-traversal-X7; @fig-vae-traversal-X2; @fig-vae-traversal-X8].

*X7 — Height/Width ratio (the diplomatic-tradition axis).* Latent traversal of X7
produces the clearest geometric transition: from a tall, narrow portrait tablet at
high X7 values to a wide, compact landscape tablet at low X7 values. The primary
descriptor is the h/w ratio itself for all three genre baselines, confirming X7 as
the pure orientation axis. Yet X7 is not a diachronic trend: it separates scribal
*traditions* rather than temporal *positions*. Neo-Assyrian (X7 = +2.05) and Early
Dynastic I-II (X7 = +1.86) are both deeply portrait traditions, despite being
separated by two millennia; Achaemenid (X7 = −2.48) and Middle Babylonian (X7 =
−1.79) are both landscape traditions, despite emerging at different periods and
from very different institutional contexts. X7 encodes the *what* of tablet shape:
which diplomatic tradition produced a given document, regardless of when.

*X2 — Bounding-box fill efficiency (the diachronic-drift axis).* X2 traversal
produces a subtler but historically richer transition. At low X2, the decoded
silhouette is a tall, narrow portrait shape with an articulated, multi-lobed outline
— reflecting the irregular, cushion-like forms characteristic of 3rd-millennium
tablets, many of which carry separately impressed column lines, header panels,
and rounded corners that fragment their bounding-box area. At high X2, the decoded
silhouette becomes wide, compact, and rectangular, filling its bounding box
efficiently. The primary descriptor is area fraction (for Administrative and Legal
genres) or solidity (for Literary tablets), confirming that X2 captures the degree
to which the tablet fills its enclosing rectangle — a property that correlates with
but is not identical to orientation. This explains why X2 is the strongest diachronic
trend: the 3rd-to-1st-millennium transition involved not only a rotation from portrait
to landscape but a simultaneous regularization of tablet outlines from irregular,
articulated forms toward smooth, flat, slab-like rectangles. X7 measures only
the rotation; X2 measures both the rotation and the regularization together. Because
the regularization is a stronger and more consistent long-run signal than the rotation
alone, X2 tracks history better.

The genre-inconsistency of X2 — its primary descriptor is area fraction for
Administrative and Legal tablets but solidity for Literary tablets — is not a
failure of the analysis. It reflects a genuine difference in what "efficient bounding-
box use" means across scribal traditions: for administrative scribes, the key
variable is how tightly the text mass fills the available clay surface; for literary
scribes, who arrange multi-column text on larger tablets with more varied layouts,
the equivalent property is measured differently by the VAE's decoder.

*X8 — Body unity (the silhouette-cohesion axis).* X8 traversal produces a transition
from a segmented, articulated silhouette — characteristic of composite CDLI photographs
showing obverse, reverse, and edge views in a single frame, or of tablets with
pronounced waist contours — toward a unified, solid slab form. The decreasing trend
of X8 across time (ρ = −0.573) therefore has two possible interpretations: (a) a
real change from the more rounded, articulated clay bodies of the 3rd and early
2nd millennium toward the flatter, more slab-like forms of the 1st millennium, and
(b) an increasing proportion of simple single-face photographs in the CDLI image set
for later periods, with fewer composite multi-view layouts. Both processes are likely
operating simultaneously, and their contributions cannot be fully separated from
this analysis.

**Discriminative structure of the full bottleneck.** Beyond X2, X7, and X8, four
additional dimensions carry large-effect period discrimination (η² ≥ 0.15): X12,
X6, X4, and X10. None of these shows a significant linear temporal trend, indicating
that they encode orthogonal sources of variation — likely genre norms, regional
scribal traditions, or specific period-distinctive features (rounded versus squared
corners, curvature patterns) that discriminate categories without evolving directionally.
The aggregate picture is of a 12-dimensional latent space in which time-directed
evolution occupies two to three dimensions and categorical cultural identity occupies
the remainder.

**Diplomatic genealogies: hierarchical clustering.** Hierarchical clustering of
the 21 period mean vectors in the VAE latent space produces a dendrogram that groups
periods by overall shape similarity rather than by date, and in doing so recovers
several historically established diplomatic genealogies (@fig-vae-dendrogram).
Three clusters emerge consistently: (1) Neo-Babylonian, Achaemenid, and Hellenistic
periods form a tight cluster, reflecting the well-documented institutional continuity
of Babylonian administrative and temple-archive practice across the 1st millennium
[@jursaDiplomaticsLateBabylonian2021; @waerzeggers_marduk-remanni_2014;
@hacklMaterialienZurUrkundenlehre2013]; (2) Ur III, Early Old Babylonian, and Old
Babylonian form a broader cluster centered on the Babylonian portrait tradition; and
(3) Neo-Assyrian stands apart from both, its mean vector driven by the extreme
positive X7 value that distinguishes the Assyrian epistolary tradition's narrow
portrait tablets from all contemporary and preceding practice
[@radnerRelationFormat1995; @cancik-kirschbaumMiddleAssyrian2012]. Middle Elamite
remains a persistent outlier, anchored to landscape format in a period when the rest
of the 2nd-millennium world was portrait-dominant. The dendrogram does not simply
reproduce the scholar-assigned chronological order; it recovers diplomatic affiliations.

### Widget case study: interpolating between Ur III and Achaemenid administrative practice {#sec-casestudy}

To demonstrate that the VAE latent space supports genuine historical inference rather
than mere pattern recognition, we trace the morphological path between two contrasting
scribal traditions using the purpose-built interactive exploration tools.

The comparison is between the mean latent vector of Ur III administrative tablets
and that of Achaemenid administrative tablets — two of the largest and most
institutionally significant assemblages in the corpus, separated by roughly 1,600
years. Their mean vectors differ substantially across three dimensions:

- **X2**: Ur III administrative mean = −0.995; Achaemenid = +0.652 (Δ = +1.647)
- **X7**: Ur III administrative mean = −0.612; Achaemenid = −2.484 (Δ = −1.872)
- **X8**: Ur III administrative mean = −0.193 (corpus avg); Achaemenid = −0.660 (Δ = −0.467)

The X2 shift confirms the portrait-to-landscape rotation and accompanying outline
regularization (fill efficiency). The X7 shift is especially significant: both
periods are already in the portrait-leaning range of X7 (positive for Ur III,
strongly negative for Achaemenid), meaning both have a characteristic orientation,
but their positions on the orientation axis are at opposite extremes. Achaemenid
tablets are not merely more landscape than Ur III tablets in absolute proportions;
they occupy a distinct zone of the orientation axis that no other period reaches.
The X8 shift further indicates that Achaemenid tablets have more unified, slab-like
outlines than their Ur III counterparts.

When these differences are visualized through the latent interpolation widget — which
decodes synthetic tablet images at evenly spaced points along a straight line between
the two mean vectors in the 12-dimensional space — the morphological path is
historically legible. The starting image (Ur III administrative) is a moderately
portrait, gently cushioned form with slightly rounded corners and a subtly articulated
outline. Moving along the interpolation path, the silhouette first becomes more
portrait (as X7 changes), then widens and flattens (as X2 increases), then loses
outline articulation (as X8 decreases), arriving at the Achaemenid image: a clearly
landscape, compactly rectangular, slab-like form. Each waypoint in the interpolation
corresponds to a coherent intermediate diplomatic format — a tablet that could, in
principle, have belonged to the transitional Middle Babylonian or Middle Elamite
periods through which this evolution passed.

The feature exploration widget — which generates a decoded image from any manually
specified latent vector — allows a trained Assyriologist to probe whether specific
diplomatic features reflect changes in individual dimensions or interactions among
several. For example, varying only X7 while holding all other dimensions at the
Ur III administrative mean produces a convincingly portrait-format Ur III-like
tablet. Varying only X2 while holding all other dimensions constant produces a
tablet whose outline regularization changes while the overall portrait orientation
is roughly preserved. These experiments confirm the dimensional independence of the
features identified by traversal analysis and demonstrate that the widgets support
the kind of controlled diplomatic comparison that conventional database-driven
methods cannot provide at scale.

### Geographic distribution of the shape shift {#sec-geographic}

The corpus-level portrait-to-landscape transition could in principle be a
compositional artifact: if the sites that dominate 1st-millennium tablet production
happen to specialize in landscape-format document types, while those dominant in the
2nd millennium specialize in portrait, then the corpus-level trend would reflect
a shift in which sites are represented rather than a real change in scribal practice
at any given location. We test this directly through a three-layer geographic
analysis, using provenience data from the CDLI catalogue, site-to-region assignments
derived from the CDLI Linked Open Data geographic ontology [@cdliContributors2024],
and a variance decomposition framework.

**Layer 1: Variance decomposition.** We assign each tablet to one of five analytical
geographic zones (Southern Mesopotamia; Central/Northern Babylonia; Assyria/Upper
Mesopotamia; Elam/Western Iran; Periphery) and decompose the overall log-ratio shift
into a within-zone component — reflecting real change in h/w ratio at sites active
in both millennia — and a compositional component reflecting changes in which zones
contribute most tablets to each millennium's sample. The within-zone component
accounts for the majority of the observed corpus-level shift, establishing that the
portrait-to-landscape transition is predominantly a real change in scribal practice
at individual production sites, not an artifact of differential site sampling
(@fig-geo-zone-shift). The finding holds after restricting analysis to Administrative
genre tablets, which controls for the possibility that genre-composition shifts
between millennia — a smaller fraction of literary tablets, a larger fraction of
administrative records — could drive the apparent format change (@fig-geo-zone-genre).

**Layer 2: Zone-level comparisons.** All five analytical zones show a shift toward
lower h/w ratios (more landscape orientation) from the 2nd to the 1st millennium,
though the magnitude varies. Southern Mesopotamia shows the largest and most
consistent shift, driven by the dramatic contrast between the portrait-dominant
Ur III and Old Babylonian assemblages and the landscape-dominant Neo-Babylonian
and Hellenistic material from the same region. Central/Northern Babylonia —
represented primarily by Sippar-Yahrurum — shows one of the largest site-level
shifts in the corpus (Cliff's *δ* = −0.700, *p* < 0.001; see below). Elam and
Western Iran, anchored by Susa and the Persepolis Fortification Archive, maintain
a landscape-leaning profile across both millennia, consistent with the long-standing
Elamite preference for wide-format administrative documents observed in the Middle
Elamite period.

**Layer 3: Site-level panel.** For the ten sites with a minimum of thirty tablets
in both the 2nd and 1st millennium subsample, we compare h/w ratio distributions
directly using Mann-Whitney *U* tests and Cliff's *δ* as effect size
(@fig-geo-site-panel; @tbl-site-shifts). Seven of the nine statistically significant
site-level comparisons show a landscape shift; the effect sizes range from moderate
to very large.

The largest shift is at Larsa (Cliff's *δ* = −0.818, *p* < 0.001), a major Babylonian
administrative centre whose 1st-millennium assemblage is dominated by Neo-Babylonian
legal and administrative documents with a strong landscape format. Kalhu (mod. Nimrud;
δ = −0.783, *p* < 0.001) and Sippar-Yahrurum (δ = −0.700, *p* < 0.001) follow,
with Nippur (δ = −0.534, *p* < 0.001) and Uruk (δ = −0.448, *p* < 0.001) also
showing large, robust effects. Critically, the Uruk result merits special attention:
Uruk contributes 323 tablets in the 2nd-millennium subsample but 4,923 in the 1st
millennium, a 15-fold ratio that makes it the largest single contributor to the
1st-millennium sample. The fact that the Uruk shift is large and significant (and not
only present because of sheer weight of numbers in the 1st millennium) confirms that
the landscape orientation of 1st-millennium tablets at Uruk is a real property of the
site's tablet-production culture at that time, and not merely a reflection of the
site's numerical dominance in the corpus.

**The Ur anomaly.** One site deviates from the general landscape trend. Ur
(mod. Tell al-Muqayyar; 170 tablets in the 2nd-millennium sample, 34 in the 1st)
shows a statistically significant shift in the *opposite* direction: from a 2nd-millennium
median h/w of 1.444 to a 1st-millennium median of 2.000 (Cliff's *δ* = +0.333,
*p* < 0.01). The most plausible explanation is a genre-composition shift: the 2nd-millennium
Ur sample is dominated by Old Babylonian administrative and legal documents, while the
much smaller 1st-millennium Ur sample contains predominantly Neo-Babylonian cultic and
temple administrative records from the sanctuary of the moon god Nanna/Sîn, a genre
and institutional context with known preferences for taller, more portrait-format
tablets. Ur in the 1st millennium was an important cult centre rather than a general
administrative hub, and its tablet corpus reflects this institutional specialization.

| Site | Zone | 2nd-mil median | 1st-mil median | Cliff's *δ* | *p* |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Larsa | S. Mesopotamia | 1.457 | 0.778 | −0.818 | < 0.001 |
| Kalhu | Assyria | 2.000 | 0.976 | −0.783 | < 0.001 |
| Sippar-Yahrurum | C./N. Babylonia | 1.388 | 0.768 | −0.700 | < 0.001 |
| Dilbat | S. Mesopotamia | 1.077 | 0.780 | −0.580 | < 0.001 |
| Nippur | S. Mesopotamia | 1.133 | 0.788 | −0.534 | < 0.001 |
| Uruk | S. Mesopotamia | 1.150 | 0.733 | −0.448 | < 0.001 |
| Kish | S. Mesopotamia | 1.306 | 1.088 | −0.135 | 0.048 |
| Assur | Assyria | 0.976 | 1.000 | −0.146 | 0.025 |
| Nineveh | Assyria | 1.143 | 1.025 | −0.136 | 0.160 |
| **Ur** | **S. Mesopotamia** | **1.444** | **2.000** | **+0.333** | **< 0.01** |

: Site-level h/w ratio shifts from 2nd to 1st millennium (sites with *N* ≥ 30 in
  both millennia). Negative Cliff's *δ* = shift toward landscape; positive =
  shift toward portrait. {#tbl-site-shifts}

**VAE Layer 3: regional trajectories in latent space.** Computing mean VAE vectors
for each zone × millennium combination and projecting onto the first two principal
components reveals structured movement across the latent space from the 2nd to the
1st millennium (@fig-geo-vae-pca). All five zones shift in the same direction —
increasing X2 (bounding-box fill efficiency, landscape drift) and decreasing X8
(body unity, slab regularization) — though the magnitude and pattern of shift vary
by zone. Southern Mesopotamia shows the longest trajectory, consistent with the
large site-level effects above. Elam/Western Iran shows relatively little change,
consistent with its already-landscape profile in the 2nd millennium. The Euclidean
distance between 2nd- and 1st-millennium mean vectors is greatest for Southern
Mesopotamia and Central/Northern Babylonia and smallest for the Periphery zone
(dominated by Anatolian sites with limited 1st-millennium representation).
Together, the three analytical layers converge on a single conclusion: the
portrait-to-landscape transition is a real, geographically widespread shift in
cuneiform scribal practice, not a sampling artifact.

     PART 5 — DISCUSSION
     ============================================================ -->

## Discussion

### Three converging signals, one historical narrative

The portrait-to-landscape transition documented in this study emerges from three
independent measurement regimes — physical pixel ratios, image-derived pixel ratios,
and VAE latent-space coordinates — and is confirmed across geographically distributed
production sites ranging from Larsa in the south to Kalhu in the Assyrian heartland.
No single technical choice drives the finding. The convergence of methods with
different potential confounds constitutes the strongest evidence of the result's
robustness.

The VAE analysis deepens the finding by revealing that this historical transition
operates along at least two separable axes in the shape space. X7, the dimension that
most sharply distinguishes between scribal traditions (η² = 0.435), measures
height/width ratio directly. X2, the most strongly diachronic dimension (ρ = +0.655),
measures bounding-box fill efficiency — a composite of orientation and outline
regularization that tracks the slow geological drift of cuneiform scribal conventions
over 3,000 years. That these two axes are distinct is itself historically informative:
it implies that the transition was not simply a rotation of tablets from tall to wide,
but involved a simultaneous and correlated change in the overall form of the clay
body — from irregular, articulated, cushion-like objects to flat, compact, rectangular
slabs. Scholars of manuscript production have argued that document format changes
involve precisely this kind of coupled transformation, in which the shift of a
"fixed balance" proportion template brings with it changes to related material
properties of the support [@georgeGeometryEarlyQuranic2010; @stokesPalaeographyDigitalAge2015].
The cuneiform evidence from this corpus is consistent with that account.

### Standardization as a proxy for institutional control

The CV-based standardization analysis yields a scale of institutional control over
scribal format that is coherent with the historical record and extends it
quantitatively. At the well-standardized end: Ur III (CV = 0.251), a state whose
administrative infrastructure is the most extensively documented in pre-Sargonic
Mesopotamia and whose centralized scribal training and accounting system is widely
recognized [@steinkellerHistoryTexts2017; @englund_administrative_1988]. The
mathematical result is that Ur III tablets are more tightly clustered around their
modal format than those of any other period in 3,300 years of cuneiform production.
This is not a trivial observation: the CV integrates the effects of scribal training,
institutional supervision, genre conventions, and the physical constraints of the
archival system into a single number. When that number is as low as 0.251, every
force that could produce format variation — individual habit, genre deviation, regional
practice — has been subordinated to a dominant institutional norm
[@eerkensStandardizationArtifact2000].

At the opposite end of the scale, the Neo-Babylonian corpus (CV = 0.807) reflects
a world in which multiple institutional actors — Babylonian temple corporations,
private banking families, provincial governors, royal administrators — were
simultaneously producing tablets within the same broad tradition but without a
shared standardizing authority imposing format uniformity. The Neo-Babylonian CV
is evidence for exactly the kind of institutional pluralism that scholars of the
period have identified through archival analysis [@jursaDiplomaticsLateBabylonian2021].
The Achaemenid period, following Neo-Babylonian, shows a partial return toward
standardization in the narrow IQR of the landscape cluster, which we read as the
imposition of imperial format norms on a pre-existing diverse Babylonian scribal
landscape — not a return to Ur III-level uniformity, but a disciplining of the
most deviant practices.

### The Achaemenid signature: continuity, empire, and the Elamite precedent

The Achaemenid period's position in the VAE dendrogram — clustered with
Neo-Babylonian and Hellenistic rather than with Middle Babylonian or earlier
Mesopotamian traditions — is consistent with a well-established scholarly
consensus on Babylonian institutional continuity under Achaemenid rule. Temple
archives continued to function under Persian governance; the same scribal families
and the same archival conventions persisted into the Persian and even early
Hellenistic periods
[@waerzeggers_marduk-remanni_2014; @hacklMaterialienZurUrkundenlehre2013;
@jursaBabylonianSources2021]. The tablet shapes reflect this continuity at the
material level.

Two further observations extend this picture. First, the Achaemenid period is
characterized by the most negative mean X7 value of any period in the corpus
(−2.484), placing it further toward landscape on the pure orientation axis than
even the Neo-Babylonian mean. This extreme position is not fully explained by
institutional continuity from Neo-Babylonian practice alone; it suggests an
additional force pulling toward landscape, for which two candidates exist. The
first is the influence of Aramaic scribal conventions: Aramaic, written on parchment
in landscape orientation, was the administrative lingua franca of the Achaemenid
empire alongside cuneiform, and the co-existence of Aramaic parchment rolls and
cuneiform clay tablets in the same administrative offices may have exerted
format-normative pressure on tablet-producing scribes toward wider, flatter forms.
We offer this as a hypothesis for investigation rather than a demonstrated conclusion,
since the relationship between writing-support norms across different media in
Achaemenid Babylonia is not yet well enough documented to permit quantitative testing.

The second candidate is the Elamite administrative tradition. The Middle Elamite
period (1,450–1,050 BCE) achieves the highest VAE X2 value in the entire corpus
(+2.902) and a median h/w of 0.863 — landscape-dominant in a period when all
contemporary Babylonian and Assyrian corpora were strongly portrait. The Achaemenid
administrative apparatus inherited Elamite precedents through the Persepolis
Fortification Archive, where Elamite scribes administered imperial rations and
stores alongside cuneiform administrative practice [@jursaAspectsTaxationAchaemenid2009].
A landscape format tradition that was already established in Elamite administrative
culture centuries before the Achaemenid period could have provided an additional
normative pressure toward landscape formats in Achaemenid Babylonia and Persia.
The geographic analysis supports this interpretation: the Elam/Western Iran zone
shows the least diachronic change in tablet shape of any zone, consistent with
a tradition that had arrived at landscape format earlier and maintained it continuously.

### The Ur anomaly: genre, function, and counter-trends

The counter-trend at Ur — where 1st-millennium tablets become *more* portrait
rather than less — illustrates the importance of institutional context for
interpreting format data. Ur in the 1st millennium was not primarily an
administrative hub of the kind that dominates the landscape-trending corpus; it
was a cult city centred on the Nanna/Sîn temple, whose cultic administrative
records, votive inscriptions, and ritual documents maintained format conventions
tied to religious practice rather than to the secular administrative bureaucracy
driving the landscape transition elsewhere. The Ur anomaly is therefore not a
counter-example to the portrait-to-landscape trend — it is evidence that the
trend was primarily an administrative and secular phenomenon, and that cultic
and temple-focused scribal contexts retained older portrait norms longer.
The capacity of this analysis to isolate such site-specific divergences, rather
than averaging them away in a corpus-level statistic, is precisely what makes
geographic disaggregation a productive complement to the aggregate trend analysis.

### Limitations

**Ratios as proxies.** Height-to-width ratios derived from photographs encode
relative proportions rather than absolute dimensions. Physical tablet dimensions
are not systematically recorded in the CDLI catalogue, and their acquisition through
standardized photogrammetric imaging would substantially reduce distributional overlap
between period categories. As noted above, our classifiers achieve performance far
above random baseline despite this information loss, which makes the case for genuine
morphological differentiation, but the overlap itself means that individual
period assignments based on ratio alone carry substantial uncertainty.

**Non-representative corpus.** The CDLI corpus reflects the cumulative priorities
of two centuries of excavation and the digitization policies of collecting
institutions, not the actual distribution of cuneiform production in antiquity.
The four most heavily represented periods account for 63% of all tablets. The
geographic analysis is constrained to sites and periods where both the
archaeological and digitization records are rich enough to yield the minimum
sample sizes required for statistical testing.

**Two-dimensional silhouettes.** The binary silhouette discards information about
tablet thickness, surface curvature, edge profile, and clay properties that are
diagnostically significant in traditional diplomatic analysis. The VAE X8 dimension
(body unity) partially recovers one element of this discarded information — the
degree of outline articulation visible in the 2D projection — but 3D morphometric
data, increasingly available through photogrammetric documentation of cuneiform
collections, would substantially enrich the feature space available for analysis.

**Periodization as a convention.** The 21 period categories used as training labels
are scholarly constructs with imprecise boundaries. The classifier's confusion
between adjacent periods — particularly Early Old Babylonian and Old Babylonian —
is partly a reflection of this boundary imprecision rather than a failure of the
model to detect shape differences. Periods defined by scholarly convention may
differ from the actual temporal structure of format change in the underlying
tablet-production record.

<!-- ============================================================
     PART 6 — CONCLUSIONS
     ============================================================ -->

## Conclusions

Cuneiform tablets are physical objects as well as textual documents, and their
physical form is a historical signal as well as a material support. Across 94,936
images spanning 3,300 years, we have demonstrated that the two-dimensional silhouette
of a cuneiform tablet carries sufficient historical information to identify its period
of origin with approximately 61% macro-F1 accuracy across 21 classes — approximately
86% of the classification signal present in the full photographic image, at a 4.8%
random baseline. This result establishes, for the first time at population scale,
that tablet shape *alone* is a quantitatively tractable diplomatic criterion.

The flagship empirical finding is the three-millennium shift from portrait to
landscape tablet orientation. A corpus whose 3rd-millennium tablets cluster at median
h/w ratios of 1.1–1.3 gives way, through a protracted transition in the Middle
Babylonian and Middle Elamite periods, to a 1st-millennium corpus whose dominant
productions — Neo-Babylonian, Achaemenid, Hellenistic — cluster at 0.74–0.90.
Geographic disaggregation confirms that this shift is real and widespread: it is
present at the site level in Southern Mesopotamia, Central/Northern Babylonia, and
the Assyrian heartland simultaneously, and the variance decomposition establishes
that it is not an artifact of differential site sampling across millennia.

Three further contributions refine this finding. The CV-based standardization scale
quantifies institutional control over scribal format: Ur III (CV = 0.251) stands as
the most tightly standardized tablet-producing context in the corpus, consistent
with the centralized training and bureaucratic infrastructure of the Third Dynasty
of Ur, while Neo-Babylonian (CV = 0.807) reflects the institutional pluralism of
the late first millennium. Achaemenid tablets exhibit a partial re-standardization
in landscape format (narrow IQR = 0.150), consistent with imperial format norms
imposed on a diverse pre-existing Babylonian scribal landscape — with additional
normative pressure possibly contributed by the concurrent Aramaic scribal tradition
and the long-established Elamite landscape format. The VAE analysis adds structural
resolution to the aggregate trend: the 12-dimensional latent space separates the
diachronic drift in tablet form (encoded in X2: bounding-box fill efficiency) from
the categorical identity of diplomatic traditions (encoded in X7: height/width ratio
directly), establishing that scribal-tradition identity and temporal position are,
in the language of the learned feature space, largely orthogonal sources of variation.

The methodology demonstrated here — distant viewing of document silhouettes,
combined with VAE-based interpretable feature extraction and geographic disaggregation
— is transferable to any ancient document corpus where material form encodes
cultural history. Papyrus roll dimensions in the Hellenistic world, parchment quire
proportions in medieval codex production, and oracle bone formats in Shang-dynasty
China are all candidates for this style of analysis as their respective corpora
become digitally accessible at comparable scale. The specific contribution of this
study to cuneiform scholarship is to demonstrate that diplomatic analysis, the
systematic study of document format as historical evidence, can now be conducted at
a scale — nearly 100,000 objects, 21 historical periods, 3,300 years — that was
previously available only to computational methods. The implicit, individually
exercised expertise of the traditional diplomat becomes, in this framework, explicit,
reproducible, and scalable.

<!-- ============================================================
     PART 7 — MATERIALS AND METHODS
     ============================================================ -->

## Materials and Methods

**Dataset.** The working corpus of 94,936 tablet images was assembled from the CDLI
catalogue [@cdliContributors2024], filtering to entries with photographic documentation
of sufficient image quality, confirmed period assignments in the CDLI metadata taxonomy,
and a minimum of 50 specimens per period class. Period labels follow the CDLI standard
taxonomy of 21 categories. Genre labels were used for genre-stratified analyses
(Administrative, Literary, Legal) and for the CV standardization sub-analysis;
these also follow CDLI metadata fields. The dataset, including all extracted ratio
measurements, VAE encodings, and period/genre metadata, is publicly available
[@zenodoDataset].

**Silhouette extraction.** Each image was converted to grayscale, subjected to Otsu's
thresholding [@otsuThresholdSelectionMethod1979], and processed with morphological
closing to fill surface-engraving holes. The largest connected component was extracted
as the tablet silhouette. Height-to-width ratios were derived from the bounding box
of this silhouette. Full pipeline details and code are available in the project
repository.

**Classification models.** The decision tree operates on scalar h/w ratio alone.
The CNN and ResNet50 [@heResNet2016] were trained with standard cross-entropy loss
and evaluated on a held-out test set. ResNet50 was fine-tuned from ImageNet pretrained
weights. All models use the same train/test split (80/20, stratified by period).
Macro-averaged F1 is reported for comparability across imbalanced 21-class settings.

**VAE.** The Variational Autoencoder [@kingmaVAE2013] was trained on 94,936 masked
silhouettes (80×80 pixels, grayscale) with a 12-dimensional bottleneck and a combined
reconstruction plus KL-divergence loss, augmented with a classification auxiliary
loss over the 21 period categories to encourage period-discriminative structure in
the latent space. The trained model checkpoint is publicly available [@zenodoModels].
Latent encodings for all 94,936 tablets are available as part of the dataset release
[@zenodoDataset].

**VAE traversal analysis.** For each of the three statistically significant
diachronic dimensions (X2, X7, X8), a traversal was constructed by fixing all other
dimensions at the genre-specific global mean and varying the target dimension across
its ±2σ range in 11 equally spaced steps. Five geometric descriptors (h/w ratio,
area fraction, solidity, compactness, eccentricity) were measured on the decoded
binary silhouette at each step, normalized 0–1 per traversal, and used to identify
the primary descriptor as the one with the highest monotonic association with the
traversal axis (assessed via Spearman ρ). Three genre baselines (Administrative,
Literary, Legal) were traversed separately to assess genre consistency.

**Statistical methods.** Period-level significance for VAE dimensions was assessed
with the Kruskal-Wallis H test; effect size η² = (H − k + 1) / (N − k).
Diachronic trend was assessed with Spearman rank correlation of period mean values
against chronological rank order. Adjacent-period and millennium-level h/w comparisons
used the Mann-Whitney *U* test with Cliff's *δ* as effect size.
For geographic site-level comparisons, Bonferroni correction was applied within
the set of tested sites.

**Geographic region assignment.** Provenience strings from the CDLI catalogue were
matched against the CDLI Linked Open Data geographic ontology (`places.nt`;
CDLI Network), which encodes 737 provenience entities and site-to-region
containment relationships for 245 of them, derived from the Pleiades ancient world
gazetteer. Five sites absent from the automated lookup but present in the 2nd–1st
millennium corpus were assigned manually by the authors following standard
historical-geographic references. Full documentation and the supplementary site
table (Table S-Geo) are provided in the Supplementary Information.
